content: Flock worker's lung (FWL) is a rare interstitial lung disease that manifests as lymphocytic bronchiolitis and peribronchiolitis in individuals exposed to flock fibers. Flock fibers are short synthetic fibers, typically made from materials like nylon, rayon, or polypropylene, which are cut from long filaments and applied to adhesive-coated substrates to create a fuzzy, carpet-like texture. The disease was first identified in 1998 when workers at a flocking plant developed interstitial lung disease of unknown origin. Initially, these cases were misdiagnosed as desquamative pneumonia and attributed to unspecified toxin exposure. However, subsequent cases revealed a clear association with flock fiber exposure, with clinical findings best characterized as lymphocytic bronchiolitis. Patients typically present with progressive dyspnea, dry cough, and constitutional symptoms, with some experiencing work-related symptom exacerbation early in the disease course. Historically, concerns about respiratory risks associated with synthetic fibers like polyester, nylon, and acrylic dust have been raised since 1975. Early assessments by the National Institute of Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) in the 1970s and 1980s linked respiratory symptoms among workers to the irritant properties of non-respirable flock fibers affecting the upper airways but did not explore the possibility of interstitial lung disease. In the 1990s, cases of cough and dyspnea were reported among workers in nylon flock handling plants in Ontario and Rhode Island. Initially, these cases were thought to be work-related hypersensitivity pneumonitis. However, further investigations identified eight cases of interstitial lung disease among approximately 150 workers at the Rhode Island plant by 1998. Histopathological findings from biopsied cases ruled out hypersensitivity pneumonitis and suggested an inflammatory and possibly immunological response to a respiratory toxicant. Previous misattributions of the disease to mycotoxins in contaminated adhesives were also corrected. The pathophysiology of FWL involves the inhalation of airborne flock dust, which contains respirable fibers generated during the cutting process. These fibers can trigger interstitial lung disease. Toxicological studies have shown that ultrafine nylon fragments can cause acute inflammatory lung injury in animal models. Additionally, elevated serum levels of inflammatory mediators like IL-8 and TNF-α have been observed in polypropylene flocking workers, correlating negatively with lung diffusion capacity (DLCO). These findings suggest that IL-8 and TNF-α play key roles in the inflammatory lung injury seen in FWL. FWL is caused by occupational exposure to airborne nylon fibers, which are used in the production of upholstery, automotive products, carpets, and apparel. Differentiating FWL from other interstitial lung diseases requires a detailed history of occupational exposure and work environment. Cases have been reported in the United States, Canada, Turkey, and Spain. Studies have shown that respiratory symptoms in flock workers are not significantly associated with age, sex, tobacco use, or years of employment but are strongly correlated with increased exposure to respiratory dust, longer working hours, and specific tasks like cleaning with compressed air. The natural history of FWL varies. Some patients experience complete symptom resolution, while others develop permanent restrictive pulmonary function deficits or progressive pulmonary deterioration, leading to respiratory failure and death. Low baseline lung diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) is associated with disease progression. Steroid therapy and cessation of nylon exposure can lead to symptomatic improvement over months or years, but some patients may require chronic supplemental oxygen or experience recurrent dyspnea. There is also an increased risk of lung cancer in affected individuals. Diagnosis of FWL is based on histological findings of non-specific interstitial pneumonia with bronchiolocentric lymphoid infiltration, interstitial fibrosis, and macrophage alveolar filling. High-resolution CT scans are highly sensitive for detecting characteristic findings like ground-glass opacities and micronodules. Pulmonary function tests typically reveal restrictive ventilatory defects. Transbronchial biopsy may aid in ruling out alternative diagnoses, but wedge biopsy is often necessary for definitive diagnosis. Treatment involves cessation of nylon exposure and corticosteroid therapy to manage respiratory symptoms. However, lung function may continue to decline in some cases. Prevention strategies include reducing worker exposure to flock dust through engineering controls, alternative cleaning methods, improved cutter maintenance, and medical surveillance programs. NIOSH has made recommendations to manufacturers to implement these measures, which have successfully reduced the number of reported cases.
